first.text: At the end of the long walk, where the last board lies crooked in the water, a big man sits on a sedge tussock with his boots in the mere. A ship's lantern stands lit beside him, its horn panes gold. He is whittling.
A bit of red cord is knotted at his belt.
He doesn't look up. The shavings fall on the water and float there; nothing out here moves them.
Mind that last board. It's laid for going in, not for coming back. Nobody lays them the other way.
You can open your hand. I'm sat by a lit one already.
That's a bare light you carry. Don't mind it on my account. I've my own now.
You called me, out at the Heron's foot. I heard. I nearly turned. It wasn't time.
You were at the Heron's foot with the eel-man, and you let me go without a word. That was kindly.
You were at the Heron's foot. You looked at me like I was weather. That was kindly too, in its way.
Somebody tied this on the letting post with a strip of sailcloth. "The stool's still by the door." Only one person alive says a thing that flat. That was you carried it.
Somebody hung word on the letting post: someone from Saltmarrow came looking. I cut it off the hook. Then I went back for it. That was you, I'd guess.
There was nothing on the letting post for me. I looked, every day, and there was nothing, and that was the best of it.
Tollen. Dunstan Tollen, of Saltmarrow, once.
The name goes past you like rain off a coat. Saltmarrow stays; the rest won't.
My sister keeps the harbor there. Mara. You'll have met her, if you came through.
Mara's brother, who went north with a lantern, laughing.
And you're the one lit the Heron. I was stood at the fog's foot when it took. I held this up, and it caught. Same as the keeper's bell, I'd guess. Nobody struck it.
Hesper's gone without her name, then. She's kept mine, mind. Wouldn't give mine to it.
And the old eel-man's cord went in. Seventy years of turnings. He'll not forgive the fen for it, nor you, and he'll be glad of the light every night he's left.
How's Mara?
How is she? Mara?

choice.text: She sent word: the stool's still by the door.
It was me tied her word on the post. She meant it.
She says Tollens end with her. And she keeps setting out two cups.
She's well. She keeps the harbor, and everyone fed.
She's well. She keeps the harbor, and everyone fed.
That's not mine to carry out here.

message.text: You give it him the way she gave it you: the stool, the door, and the last part too. Don't tell him to come home. He knows where it is.
He laughs: one great laugh like a dropped anchor, and the fog doesn't carry it anywhere.
There. That's Mara all over. Tells you not to, so you'll know she would.

message_post.text: I know she did. I've worn it since. Half of it, anyway. The other half's round a gull's neck, up the Heron.

gift.text: He turns the thing he's been whittling over in his fingers, a gull no bigger than a thumb, and blows the shavings off it.
Take her this. Set it on the stool. Not facing north, like the other. Facing the door.
And tell her it's not a promise. It's only so she knows I know where it is.

burned.text: So the Gull's light took her keeping of me. That's what it ate, your lighting it.
Then she's put me down before I've put her down. That's backward.
He laughs, and it comes out smaller than he meant.
Tollens always did go backward. I rowed here facing the wrong way. Don't take her anything of mine. Two cups out is enough of me for anyone.

spared.text: He looks at you a moment longer than the words need, and lets it go.

well.text: She would be. Whole harbor fed, and nobody's thanked her once.

nothing.text: Fair. Not mine either, out here. That's the idea.

choice.text: What's the lantern for?
What did you come here to put down?
I won't ask what you came here for.
Is it you who climbs the Heron's ladder?
I'll leave you to it.

lantern.text: When I've done. You can't walk out of the Deeps in the dark. Nobody can; the boards only go the one way. I'll want to see where I'm putting my feet. So I waited on the Heron.
Nearly. That's the trouble with it. I don't know how much there was, so I can't tell how much is left.
When I am, I'll walk back in with this and ask Hesper for my name. Not before.

asked.text: That's the one rule here, and you've broke it sat on the last board.
He laughs, the dropped-anchor laugh, and goes back to the gull.
I'll tell you anyway, since you asked it honest. I don't know. That's how you know it went.
I laughed all the way up the coast because it was going to stop. Whatever it was. That much I kept: that it was going to stop.

kept.text: Good. Hesper'll have told you the rule. Not many keep it out here, where there's nobody to see.
Sit a minute, if you like. The light's good.

climb.text: Some nights. Somebody ought to sit up with them, up there. They're cold.
I didn't carry them up. They were there the first time I climbed, and there's more each time I go. I don't know whose. I don't ask. That's the rule.
The gull's mine. I set it on the rim so they'd have something keeping watch.
The coat was folded when I came. I never touched it. Some things you leave the way they were left.

again.text: Dunstan sits at the end of the long walk with his boots in the mere and the lantern lit beside him, whittling.
The big man sits at the end of the long walk with his boots in the mere and the lantern lit beside him, whittling.
You've still got that gull. No hurry. She's not going anywhere, and nor's the stool.

walk_back.text: Halfway along the long walk a big man stands on a board with the lantern held out in front of him, lit. He's facing in, toward Stillhithe. He isn't moving.
There you are. I'd a feeling it'd be you. Nobody else out here goes about with a light on purpose.
Done. I think. There's nothing left out there I'd know to look for, and I looked a good while.

Here's the trouble. Every board on this walk is laid by somebody going in. The near edge sits proud, the far edge sinks. You walk them out, they carry you. You walk them back, they tip you in the mere.
A lantern's no good for that. A lantern shows you where you are. I want somebody ahead of me showing me where the next one is.
You'd have to open your hand, mind. Just this once, out here. They'll forgive you; you're walking a man in.
You've a gull of mine in your satchel still. Hang on to it a bit longer.

choice.text: Walk ahead of him with the ember.
Not yet. Wait here.

wait.text: I've waited worse places. Bring the light when you've a mind to.

walking_in.text: You go first, the ember held low, and find each board before he needs it. He comes on behind, slow, testing every one, the lantern swinging, and he talks the whole way about nothing: weather, eels, a boat he once nearly bought.

You open your hand. The light comes out gold over the water, and you go first, the ember held low, finding each board before he needs it. He comes on behind, slow, testing every one, and he talks the whole way about nothing: weather, eels, a boat he once nearly bought.
By the pools, the Unmoored turn their faces from your light, the way they do. When they see who walks behind it, one or two turn back to look.
Let them look. Somebody walking out of the Deeps. They'll want to know it can be done, even the ones who'll never try it.
At Stillhithe's edge he steps off the last board onto the hummock and stands a while with both feet on the ground, as if he'd forgotten how it goes.
Right. The staithe. I'll ask her myself; that's how it's kept.

his_name.text: Dunstan stands at the staithe's foot in front of Hesper with his lantern in one hand and his other hand open, the way you'd stand at a counter to collect a thing you'd paid for.
I've come for my name, Hesper. I said I'd not, before I was done. I'm done.
You're sure. I'll not keep it twice.
Sure as I'll ever be. I don't know how much there was. I know there's none left I'd miss.
She takes it out from somewhere under the shawl, as though she'd carried it in a pocket, and says it once, carefully, the way you'd hand back a full cup.
I couldn't keep my own. I've still got yours. Here.
It goes past you like rain off a coat. You hear it said, and then you only know that something was. He heard it, though. You can see him hear it.
That's the one. Fits worse than I remember. It'll wear in.
He laughs, the dropped-anchor laugh, and this time the fog carries it a little way.
And now I don't know what a Tollen does next. I'd not thought past this bit. That was rather the point of it.
Boat's where I left it. Tide's nothing here; water doesn't move. I could row her anywhere.

choice.text: Go home. Mara's keeping the stool.
There's a second cup going cold by her door. Go home and drink it.
Stay a while. Till you're sure it's done.
That's yours to choose. Not mine.

go_home.text: Keeping it. She would be. Swept round it, not under it, I'd lay money.

go_home_cup.text: She'll not know me. You said. The light took her keeping of me.
Well. Then I'll be a stranger who knows where the cups go. There's worse things to be. Somebody ought to drink the other one.

yours.text: Mine, is it. Nobody's said that to me since I was nine.
He looks south, where the lanes run, a long time.
Home, then. A Tollen goes backward. I'll row her home facing this way, and watch the fen go.

rowing.text: Give us that gull back. I'll set it on the stool myself. Facing the door; I know.

He steps down into the rowboat at the staithe's first post, ships the oars, sets the lantern in the stern, and pulls out stroke by stroke, sitting the wrong way round the way sea-folk do, so he can watch where he's been.
First one ever went out of here by the staithe. They all go by the long walk.
Tell Oda I'm not laughing at the weather. I'm laughing at something else. She'll want to know.

stay.text: Sure it's done. Aye. I'd not want to row all the way to Saltmarrow and find a bit left in the bilge.
And I'll tell you what I'll do while I'm sure. I'll turn the boards. Every one on that walk, laid the other way round, so the next one coming back can walk it without a light.
Nobody mends anything here. Mending's remembering.
I know. I've finished forgetting. Somebody may as well start the other thing.

stayed.text: Dunstan stands at the head of the long walk with the lantern in his fist and a lifted board at his feet, turning the boards one by one so the near edge sits proud for coming back.
The big man stands at the head of the long walk with the lantern in his fist and a lifted board at his feet, turning the boards one by one so the near edge sits proud for coming back.
Two turned so far, and the rest to come. Some of them come off their tussocks and watch me do it. Nobody's said a word. That's the rule, I suppose.
When it's done I'll know it's done. Then Saltmarrow. Tell her that if you're passing. Or don't. She'll know where I am, by the stool.
When it's done I'll know. Then I'll go and drink that cup.

choice.text: Oda says the Mercy will carry you home when you're done. No fare.
I'll leave you to it.

home.text: Dunstan Tollen sits on his stool by Mara's door, his sea boots planted on the harbor stones, a cup held in both hands between his knees. The dent in the seat fits him exactly.
The big man sits on the stool by Mara's door, his sea boots planted on the harbor stones, the second cup held in both hands between his knees. The dent in the seat fits him exactly.
Came in backward. Whole harbor stood on the wall to watch, and Tam rang the gate bell like I was a fire. Mara never came down. She was setting the stool square.
Gull's on the sill, facing the door. I sat on it the first night. She's not let me forget that, and she won't.
She doesn't know me. She poured that second cup and pushed it at me and said it was going cold anyway. So I drank it.
I've told her I'm her brother. She says Tollens end with her. I say that's all right, then: I'll be the bit after the end. She let that stand. It's a start.
Still don't know what it was I put down. Still glad. Ask me again in a year.

choice.text: Oda says your berth's still swung on the Slow Mercy.
Was it worth the walk back?
I'll leave you to your cup.

worth.text: Walking out was the easy half. Anybody can walk out; the boards are laid for it.
Coming back you need somebody ahead of you with a light. I'd not have found the boards. So it's yours as much as mine, whatever it was worth.

choice.text: I'll leave you to your cup.

berth.text: He laughs: once, from low down, like an anchor going over.
Swung, is it. Two winters on that deck and she never once let me finish a verse.
No. Tell her no, and thank you, and tell her it's a stool now. She'll know what I mean by a stool.
And... it's a comfort, somebody on the water knowing my face. Don't tell her I said comfort. She'd never let me aboard again.
He settles the cup back between his knees.

choice.text: I'll tell her.

no_fare.text: He sets the board down and wipes his hands on his coat, slowly, as if he wants to be sure of them.
I came out by oar. I'll go home by oar; a Tollen finishes what he starts, even backward. But tell her I heard it.
And tell her I'll wave from the staithe every time the Mercy goes by. Every time. Till she's sick of it.

choice.text: I'll tell her.
